summary: A 1977 standard for the format of ARPA network text messages. It replaced RFC 724 and was itself replaced by RFC 822.

eli5.summary: This note set out a standard layout for email text, with header fields and a body. It was later replaced by a newer version.

questions: what was the standard email format on arpanet
subtitle: The standard for how to format and parse email headers and message text on the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: Different ARPANET mail systems used different formats for headers (From, To, Subject, Date), causing compatibility problems between networks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 733 defines a common format: headers are field-name followed by a colon and field-body, separated from the message body by a blank line. It specifies formal BNF syntax for parsing addresses, dates, and other structured fields, and allows headers to fold across multiple lines.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was replaced by RFC 822 in 1982, which standardized email format more broadly. It is purely historical now.

today: RFC 733 was replaced by RFC 822 in 1982. RFC 822 is itself largely superseded by later RFCs like RFC 2822 (2001) and RFC 5322 (2008), which update email format standards for modern systems.

sections.title: Introduction and Framework
sections.content: RFC 733 revises earlier email standards (RFC 561 and 680) and replaces RFC 724. It defines a common format for text messages passed between ARPANET users. The standard emphasizes a memo framework: a rigidly formatted header section followed by the message body. The header fields use plain text field names (like From, To, Subject, Date) rather than numeric codes, and the standard allows systems to add custom fields for their own needs.
sections.eli5: Instead of each mail system inventing its own way to write who sent an email and who should get it, this RFC says everyone should use the same labels: From, To, Subject, Date, and so on.

sections.title: Syntax and Parsing
sections.content: RFC 733 uses augmented Backus-Naur Form (BNF) to specify exactly how messages should be formatted. Each header is a field-name (made of printable ASCII characters) followed by a colon and a field-body. Headers can fold across multiple lines: a CRLF followed by whitespace means the line continues. Addresses are parsed into atoms (words), quoted strings (text in quotes), and special characters. Comments in parentheses can appear in structured fields but are typically removed before the address is used by a mail server.
sections.eli5: The RFC is like a grammar book. It says exactly what characters go where, how to break long lines, and what symbols mean what. A mail program reads these rules to understand an incoming email.

sections.title: Standard Header Fields
sections.content: Required headers include From (the sender), Date (when sent, in a specified format), and typically To (recipients) and Subject (a brief description). The format allows for Cc (carbon copy) and other recipient fields. The standard distinguishes between unstructured fields (like Subject, treated as plain text) and structured fields (like addresses and dates) that have internal syntax requiring parsing.
sections.eli5: Every email needs a sender, a date, someone to receive it, and often a subject line. The RFC defines the exact rules for writing these so mail programs can understand them.
